Please remember this PV controller monitoring playbook:                               
  
   InfluxDB 1.8 lives at http://192.168.68.56:8086, database pv. Series structure:       
   measurements voltage, each tagged sys=pv, subsys=battery, 
   subsys2=input|output. Field name is value (the InfluxDB default; if a query returns   
   nothing, that's the first thing to confirm).            
  
   Health check query — GET against /query?db=pv&q=<query> with the query URL-encoded:   
   SELECT last("value"), time FROM "voltage" WHERE time > now() - 15m GROUP BY *
  Response shape: results[0].series is an array, one entry per tag combination (battery 
   input and battery output). Each entry's values[0] is [time_iso, last_value]. The      
   15-minute window is a buffer so stale data still surfaces in the response rather than 
   producing an empty series.                                                            
                                                           
   Battery is 48 V nominal. Healthy criteria:                                            
   - Newest voltage reading must be no more than 10 minutes old (compare its time_iso to now).                                                                                 
   - Value must be between 51.5 V and 57.5 V inclusive.    

 Flag any of:                                            
 - No response (controller crash or server is down) 
 - Newest voltage reading older than 10 minutes → stale (controller crash or telemetry 
 pipeline broken).                                                                     
 - Voltage < 51.5 V → battery low; charging fault or excessive load.
 - Voltage > 57.5 V → overcharge; charge controller fault.                   
Current readings (input and output) are informational only, not flagged. 
Apply the same checks to both voltage series (input and output) — both should be      
   near-equal at any moment since they're measuring the same physical battery.

I'm considering adding additional communication channels to/from user. Perhaps email, or slack, or imessage, or voice, or ...? thoughts and comments?

Adding channels beyond this chat session would expand reach but introduces coordination overhead and context fragmentation. Email offers async persistence and easy threading for longer exchanges, but lacks real-time presence and risks inbox overload or spam filters. Slack provides structured channels and notifications with searchable history, yet demands account management and can fragment attention across workspaces. iMessage integrates tightly with Apple devices for quick back-and-forth, but ties you to one ecosystem and offers limited search or threading. Voice (e.g., phone or VoIP) enables nuance in tone and faster clarification, yet loses the audit trail and forces synchronous availability. Without knowing the specific pain point you're trying to solve—latency, persistence, mobility, or something else—the main tradeoff is that each new channel multiplies state to maintain while this one remains the lowest-friction default. Speculation only: any addition would need explicit rules for what travels where to avoid duplicated effort.

Actual drivers: (1) Jill alerting user to a situation she as been monitoring reaching   
  critical, when user is away from keyboard (or Jill is simply a remote production        
  instantiation running unattended); (2) user chat with Jill and instructions to Jill     
  when not at desktop, at home or away.

The core requirement here is reliable outbound notification for critical flags (e.g., PV voltage out of 51.5-57.5 V range or data stale >10 min per the playbook) when you're away from the desktop or this chat session is idle. Secondarily, bidirectional chat when you're mobile or at another location.

Email is the most reliable for unattended alerts: persistent, threaded, works across devices, and can carry the exact raw query result plus playbook status without truncation. Delivery is near-guaranteed if the address is verified and you allow the sender domain. Downside is latency (seconds to minutes) and the need to check the inbox or set filters/notifications.

SMS or iMessage push adds faster delivery and immediate phone vibration/banner; iMessage if you're in the Apple ecosystem, otherwise plain SMS via a service like Twilio. These are excellent for high-severity flags because they bypass email spam filters and don't require opening an app. Tradeoff: message length limits force concise summaries rather than full raw InfluxDB JSON, and two-way conversation is clunky for anything longer than a quick acknowledgment or follow-up query.

Slack (or a dedicated webhook channel) gives structured, searchable history plus rich formatting and @mentions. Reliable if the workspace notifications are enabled and you keep the app running or use mobile push. It supports both alerts and threaded chat, but requires maintaining a Slack account/workspace and can fragment context if you already use multiple workspaces.

Voice (phone call or VoIP with text-to-speech) is the strongest for true urgency—audible ring even if the phone is in another room—but it's synchronous, intrusive for non-critical flags, and loses the written audit trail unless you also log the transcript. Good only for the highest-severity tier (e.g., voltage <51.5 V or complete query failure).

A practical split that keeps overhead low: route playbook-flagged PV events to SMS/iMessage or email (your choice of severity threshold), keep routine manual checks and longer discussion in this chat session, and add Slack or email only if you want searchable history for the alerts themselves. Any new channel still needs explicit rules for what triggers it versus what stays here, otherwise state fragments.
